introduction: These readings are Bahá’u’lláh’s and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s words to Christians: to the Pope, to monks and priests, and to the people of the Gospel. They announce that the One who ascended has returned, that the Father has come and the promised Kingdom has opened, and they ask Christians to recognise Him by the Gospel’s own words and not to be held back by their leaders or their expectations. The quotations set beside them are mostly the passages the readings point to: the promises of return in the Gospels, Acts and Revelation, the voice in the wilderness, and the things that could not yet be borne. Two give the difficulty a Christian will feel at once, the Gospel’s warning against anyone who says “here is Christ” and Paul’s against another gospel, and Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor asks what a church might do if its Lord came back.
questions: The readings appeal to the Gospel’s own promises. Which of the passages set beside them would you expect a Christian reader to find most telling, and why?
Jesus warned against those who say “Lo, here is Christ”, and Paul against another gospel. How do these readings ask to be tested, and by what?
Several readings speak to monks and clergy in particular. What do they ask them to leave, and what to keep?
The Father is come, one reading says, with the word the Son concealed. What does the Gospel say about things that could not be borne at the time?
Dostoevsky imagined the church turning Christ away. What in any religious community, including one’s own, makes recognising something new from God difficult?

outside.why: The Book of Revelation announces the return in the same words as this summons: behold, he cometh with clouds.
John the Baptist described himself as a voice crying in the wilderness to make the way straight; the reading says that voice has been raised again.
Jesus spoke of a temple raised in three days, and his hearers thought only of the building of stone.
Jesus told his followers to watch, since they would not know the hour at which their Lord would come.
The Qur’an says that monasticism was something the followers of Jesus devised, seeking God's pleasure, and that they did not observe it rightly.
John's Gospel says that no one has ascended to heaven but he who came down from heaven.
The Gospel itself warns: if anyone says, Lo, here is Christ, believe it not. How is a Christian to weigh that warning against the charge of awaiting another when He has come?
The men in white at the ascension said that this same Jesus would come again in the manner in which he was seen to go.
Daniel saw one like the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, and Jesus took the phrase for himself.
Jesus reminded his disciples that he had told them beforehand: I go away, and come again unto you.
The psalm calls for the everlasting doors to be lifted up, that the King of glory may come in.
Jesus once closed the book in the synagogue of Nazareth and said: this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.
This is the saying the readings point to: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
Micah named little Bethlehem as the place from which a ruler would come forth.
Peter said for the first disciples: lo, we have left all, and have followed thee.
Dostoevsky imagined Christ returning to Seville and being told by the Grand Inquisitor that he was not wanted. What would a church have to give up to welcome the one it prays for?
Jesus said of his own coming that it was so that people might have life, and have it more abundantly.
At the last supper Jesus spoke of a day when he would drink the fruit of the vine new in his Father's kingdom.
The Qur’an says that those nearest in affection to the believers are those who say: we are Christians.
Jesus promised a Spirit of truth who would guide into all truth and would not speak of himself.
Paul told the Galatians that even an angel from heaven preaching another gospel should be refused. What distinguishes another gospel from the word the Son said could not yet be borne?
Milton could not praise a fugitive and cloistered virtue that never sallies out to meet its adversary.
